top_story: Trump’s 23 March threat to destroy Iran’s power plants unless Tehran reopened the Strait of Hormuz pushed an already expanding US-Israeli war into a sharper coercive phase, and Iranian leaders answered with vows of regional escalation that made the waterway both a military lever and a political symbol. By 28 April, the reported coordinated approval by Washington and Tehran for a sanctioned Russian oligarch’s superyacht to transit the strait showed that even amid confrontation, selective channels of deconfliction still function for elite interests. A day later, NGOs were demanding a humanitarian corridor as blockade conditions and surging oil prices choked deliveries of food, fuel, and medicine to millions, exposing how wartime control over Hormuz is falling hardest on civilians rather than power centers. The emerging picture is of a conflict that combines maximalist threats with narrow transactional exceptions, deepening the sense of US coercive overreach while intensifying regional economic and humanitarian strain.
